detailed_rationale:
NESCO runs three businesses from one Goregaon (Mumbai) campus: the Bombay Exhibition Centre, a roughly 2.5msf IT Park earning annuity rental income from tenants like HSBC, KPMG, PwC and BlackRock at 98%+ occupancy, and a small legacy engineering/bakery-equipment unit. The IT Park is the crown jewel — long-lease, high-margin, low-churn income that has historically carried group profitability — while the exhibition business is more cyclical, tied to trade-show calendars and discretionary corporate spend.

FY26 TTM sales grew 21% (3-year CAGR 20%), but TTM profit growth decelerated sharply to just 4% — a genuine margin-compression signal, not noise. The company is mid-way through a large capex program (₹753cr CWIP as of Mar 2026) funded partly by its first meaningful borrowings (₹272cr) after being essentially debt-free, presumably a new IT Park/exhibition capacity phase that isn't yet earning full-occupancy returns. Promoter holding is stable and high (68.5%), dividend payout deliberately low (~12%, cash retained for expansion), and there is no pledge or related-party red flag visible in the filings.

Quant reads this as moderate-quality (score 49), high-growth (71-82), reasonably valued (value score 70.8, 18.5x trailing PE) — consistent with a real-estate-annuity story priced sensibly, with the profit/revenue growth gap this year the main thing to monitor before crediting re-acceleration.
recommendation_rationale: Quant already reads Hold on both windows (scores ~49-50) and nothing in my research overturns that: revenue growth and underlying asset quality are genuinely good, but the multiple isn't so cheap that a 4% TTM profit growth print (against 21% sales growth) can be waved away — the new debt/capex phase needs to prove out first. No basis to rescue or escalate.
summary: NESCO owns and operates a large Mumbai exhibition-and-IT-park real estate complex, running near-full occupancy with blue-chip multinational tenants, alongside a small engineering business. Revenue has grown strongly, but profit growth has slowed this year as the company invests in new capacity, funded partly by its first meaningful borrowings in years. The core annuity business remains high quality and reasonably priced; the near-term margin dip looks like a capex-driven pause rather than a red flag, but is worth watching until the new capacity starts contributing to profit.
positive_para: A genuinely scarce asset — a large contiguous exhibition-and-office campus in central Mumbai that cannot be easily replicated — running at 98%+ IT Park occupancy with globally recognized tenants, essentially debt-free until this year, and growing revenue at a 20%+ clip for a reasonable 18.5x trailing multiple. Management is reinvesting rather than over-distributing, and promoter holding is high and stable.
negative_para: Profit growth has stalled to just 4% TTM even as sales grew 21% — real margin compression, not noise — while the company has simultaneously taken on its first material borrowings (₹272cr) to fund a large capex program (₹753cr CWIP). Until the new capacity is leased and earning full-occupancy returns, near-term earnings could stay lumpy, and the exhibition segment remains inherently more cyclical than the IT Park annuity.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At 18.5x trailing earnings for a business with a mid-teens-to-20% historical revenue growth track record and a genuine annuity core, the market isn't pricing in heroic assumptions — it roughly requires steady low-double-digit compounding, which the IT Park's occupancy and Mumbai real-estate scarcity make plausible once the current capex phase matures. Fair, tilting cheap if new capacity leases up at the quality of the existing park; the risk is execution/timing of that ramp, not the long-term asset quality.
